notes.title: Weekly Dev Diary - Issue 07
notes.content:
Wow, has it really been another week already? It's amazing how quickly the days are flying by at the moment. It has now been a full month since I started working on the electrical system (the first cables were laid on the 14th of July), so let's take a look at what progress has been made.

With the addition of the Main Stairwell and Ring 1 Radial Corridor cabling being added this week, the ship now has a total of 4.39km of active wiring, feeding 291 fully dynamic lighting panels. The images below show the extent of the wiring so far, and yet this is still just a small fraction of what will be added in the future.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/46f5220e30bbd7fd96d810ce8f04ca6700a3b59a.png

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/1995fc21217701fbebc5fdd2ed018d7d0fc9a5c3.png

The wiring isn't just there for flavour though. Every single segment of cable is carrying a live voltage, and as of this week, they are also completely interactive. The cabling now responds to damage, throwing out sparks and dropping power to end devices like the lighting. Plus, if you "accidentally" shoot the wiring, the NPC Engineers will dutifully come and repair them for you.  In the future, there will be a resource cost associated with this but for now, all repairs are free. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/286ce240109384d08dd771ebe92047cf45e80b31.png

I've also just started working on the in-game fault reporting system for the electrical distribution hardware, so when damaged cables start causing a problem the FAULT light will illuminate on the control interface.  The way this works currently is that all cabling has a health percentage, and on every electrical 'tick' the cable will roll a dice that is weighted against its health value.  The lower the health percentage gets, the more likely it is that a fault will occur.  From a gameplay perspective this means you can get away with ignoring a small amount of damage, but the longer you leave it, the more of a concern it will become for the ship and her crew.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/0e7219c932ee7de9837cc80008946f7ed136ccbd.png

So in summary, this is what the electrical system offers so far:

• A WIP fusion reactor that is producing constant power

• 48 interactive battery arrays (480 individual cells) that are feeding power into the distribution network.

• 50 interactive electrical distribution devices.

• Over 4km of interactive cabling that responds to damage.

• Upwards of 500 interactive lighting panels which both respond to damage and have multiple lighting modes.

• Over 1000 (1143 in fact) buttons you can press, which all serve an actual purpose on the ship.

• A team of NPC Engineers that autonomously fix damaged lights and cables.

notes.title: Dev Update #69
notes.content:
I've seen a few questions pop up recently asking about the travel times in Starship Simulator. This is often a topic of heated debate in space games, so I wanted to weigh in from our side and explain how we intend to handle travelling the vast distances between stars in our 1:1 scale galaxy.

Space is of course unimaginably huge, where even the light from our closest neighbouring star takes 4 years to reach us. To travel 4 lightyears we obviously need to achieve some ludicrous speeds, but we also want the journey to be meaningful, so there needs to be a balance between realistic travel time and player agency.

I've been playing and loving space games for over 30 years now, and in every example, I can think of travel between stars as relatively instant, while travelling around within a star system is fairly time-consuming. To my mind, this is completely backwards and contrary to the actual distances involved, but I do of course understand its necessity when all you have is a cockpit or bridge to interact with.

This is where Starship Simulator is different to all the other space games out there. You have an entire starship to interact with, with a number of role-relevant tasks to perform each day while on duty. This means travel between star systems doesn't need to be instant, because you're not just sat staring into space waiting to reach your destination.

The following number will likely change during playtesting, but right now we're looking at our FTL speed being roughly 5 lightyears per day. This is not just an arbitrary figure, it's actually the average distance between stars in our galaxy. It should take players about 20 minutes on average to complete their daily tasks, and typically you'll spend at least one full day at warp to get anywhere.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/a9ac59d91eced22e55f83a9cbf6d26998e26b241.png

As an interesting point of note, Earth is apparently about 26,000 lightyears from the centre of the Milky Way, which means if you were to fly there without stopping it would take you 361 days in real-time (although you would need to stop occasionally along the way to refuel). Similarly, the Milky Way is 100,000 lightyears across, so flying from one side to the other would take 3.86 years. Do we have anyone insane enough to attempt that challenge? 

The objective of the base game is to explore as far from Earth as possible, and then return home in one piece to receive accolades and recognition based on how far you managed to get, along with how many successful first contacts you were able to achieve along the way. With great risk comes great reward.

And speaking of first contacts, let's talk about travel within a star system. Ultimately this is where most of the interesting action will take place, and we want players to be able to fully explore a star system in a reasonable amount of time.  Again, this is where most games have it backwards, because if your ship is capable of covering 5 lightyears in a single day, then it could technically cover 1AU in about 0.3 seconds.

This is however where we need to "gameify" the numbers a bit because we don't want to lose that sense of scale within a star system. So, right now we're looking at speeds within a system being limited to around 0.1AU per minute. So Earth to Mars would take about 3 seconds at its closest approach, whereas Earth to Neptune would take about 3 minutes. Did I mention space is huge?

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/81f119460e086e76f92bee8e2d1cf0c47ac3fcea.png

So in summary, we want meaningful but engaging travel times between star systems, where that time is calculated based on the actual distance to the star (5ly per day), and where you'll have plenty to do on the ship to make the time pass quickly. And, we want the travel times within an individual star system to be a few minutes at most (0.1AU per minute) because we want players to be able to explore all of the available content in that system in a reasonable timeframe.

Hopefully, this approach will preserve the sheer massiveness of space, while never leaving the player sitting around with nothing to do.

notes.title: Dev Update #68
notes.content:
There's been a lot going on behind the scenes recently, so I figured it would be good to make this Dev Diary more of an overall progress update for the project. 

Soundtrack
Our composer Eric (@orchestorm) has now finished both the Main Theme and the In-Game music.  He's done a fantastic job, and both tracks will be present in the next build for backers.

Menu/Loading Screen
I've updated the main menu to include the ability to watch the ship being constructed. You'll be able to free-fly around the ship and watch in real-time as all the pieces come together and get welded into place. At the same time, I've also updated the loading screen for the demo sandbox so it looks a little more professional.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/3eb667fd648fe881db42fd0123cf7b98d0542536.png

Optimisations
Something I've learned about myself while making this game is just how obsessed I am with optimisation. I grew up with systems like the Commodore 64 and Amiga 500, and you'd get these demo discs that crammed incredible (for the time) graphics into less than 1MB of storage. It was a time when optimisation was everything, and I'm definitely finding myself looking back on those days for inspiration.

Take the main stairs for example, which contain no less than 120 blue light strips. Having 120 actual lights casting a blue glow was utter madness, so I've employed some clever mesh volumes instead which look and behave like lights, but aren't actually lights. It's this sort of trickery that enables us to produce both highly performant and great-looking environments, without having to sacrifice visual quality.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/b753209032ea3c19f99bdef57bf8bec71f23c461.png

NPC Crew
The NPC crew characters have now been updated to use Epic's new MetaHuman platform. They're incredibly realistic, but also very costly to render. It took a lot of tweaking and optimisation (980 active skeletal meshes!), but I'm happy to say we now have 196 MetaHuman characters freely roaming the ship. This was an important stress test and proof of concept, and I can now start giving them actual routines and places of work.

Right now they're all the same guy, but we'll expand that over time. You'll notice though that the shirts are different, and that's because they're using our new procedural clothing system. We'll extend this to the other items of clothing too, in addition to adding the other MetaHuman clothing items. When out of uniform, the crew are going to be rocking some sharp threads! (did I really just say that?) :D

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/c91e6d11db5888c3d14f37b430262e673a19756a.png

Engineering
We took a poll recently, asking our backers what they'd like to see development focus on next. They chose interactive engineering systems, so that's currently the primary focus of development activity.  The reactor and engineering control rooms will need to be fleshed out as part of this process, so I've started roughing out some of the interior wall panels. Essentially from this point though, every system on the ship (even the lights) will depend on the reactor being operational to function.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/07ae9ace86c98333283a5a3305c3c3b035d95d64.png

What's Next?
I found the backer poll actually worked really well, and we'll be using that approach again to drive the next phase of development. So once all the engineering systems are in a good place, we'll turn to the community once more to guide the direction of the project. Aside from addressing critical bugs (which will always be the #1 priority), I love giving the community the power to choose what they think is most important for the game. I'm pretty sure we'll continue that approach long after launch, and I'm actually excited to see what the polls will look like when the entire player base gets involved!

notes.title: Dev Update #67
notes.content:
Over the past few weeks, I've been hard at work planning the outer ring of the main habitation areas on the ship. This has proven to be quite a challenge because unlike the central part of the saucer, the outer areas are mostly large two-story rooms of various sizes.

The hardest area to fit in seamlessly has been the shuttle bay because, in contrast to the mathematically calculated ring sections of the main saucer, it's very much like trying to fit a square peg in a round hole. Almost literally in fact! But, after much trial and error, I've settled on a design that is both practical and functional, and I'm looking forward to seeing what it looks like with all the internal decor in place.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/17b688f9bdaf637bf229b584c0b0247114c81141.png

This is still very much a work in progress, but what we should end up with is 6 dedicated parking bays for various types of craft. There will likely be two crew means of transport, some small utility craft, a Mining/Resource Gathering craft, and a place to repair or construct new craft should the need arise.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/b381ab4eaebaf02f540b664365eb8e37dd8d0c8b.png

Repairing or manufacturing anything in the game will use up raw materials, so the parking bay for the mining craft will have the infrastructure in place to extract the materials and place them in storage containers for future use.  This will predominantly be for the 3D printers on the ship, which is how you'll make new parts etc.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/a1ba0efc2395130b5c1d057d719abffd65709afb.png

The shuttle bay will also have a seating area and viewing gallery on either side, and at the end of these will be a small maintenance airlock for accessing the upper hull on foot. notes.title: Dev Update #66
notes.content:
With most of the corridors now largely complete, and with doorframes in place, it's finally time to move onto the main staircase that connects decks B through F. I've been putting this off because the shapes involved are fairly complicated to model, consisting almost entirely of bends and curves. This is due to the curved nature of the deck layout, and the fact I wanted to make each staircase U-shaped instead of a spiral.  The practicality of having spiral staircases on a starship has been the subject of heated debate in the past, so I thought it best avoided 

The end result is a set of mirrored staircases that curve somewhat to match the shape of the deck structure and underlying framework:

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/b0acdedfc6fd7a143d789cbd7963c207338ef7fc.png

There will be a security desk located at the top on B Deck, controlling access to the Administration and Command areas, and at the bottom, down on F Deck, there will be a similar security desk controlling access to the Engineering areas. In order to access anything sensitive or critical on the ship, you will have to pass at least one security checkpoint.

Aesthetic-wise, I decided to use the stair design I came up with a year ago while making the very first test renders for the game. There's still a fair bit of work to do, but you should get the general idea of what it will end up looking like:

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/131809460705fa65989a77adabbe1018e8381586.png

It will eventually all be blended and moulded into the rest of the wall and ceiling panels smoothly, and I'll likely go with a glass railing with a wooden handrail on top. The stairs themselves are surrounded by a fairly large planter, which will be filled with various plants and rocks, and things.  You can never have too many plants ;)

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/20e76cd244d199a9a1982ec6b6c951fcd270df79.png

notes.title: Dev Update #65
notes.content:
A lot has happened since the last Dev Diary. To read these, please go to: https://www.patreon.com/starshipsimulator , with most of the internal decks being rotated by 45 degrees to facilitate the maintenance tunnels, and a brand new Discord server having been set up specifically for the Starsim community. Today, however, I wanted to touch on some specifics regarding air pressure on the ship and how we keep it where it's needed via its airtight doors.

To begin with, the basic framework of the ship is mass-produced with a gap left for whatever type of door will eventually be used in that location:

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/e74d62d6edbbd05234a6fa3a2aaae91a9963c93b.png

Next, the door mechanism and track are welded into place to form an airtight seal between the internal room and the corridor beyond:

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/c7980f75e5650883528ba6352da0c807285a9e9f.png

The track which holds the door could be one of various sizes, with this example being the 5cm version used on crew quarters.  Other areas of the ship, such as Engineering, will have much thicker (10cm) reinforced doors for additional security.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/540f3084c250ed4b3f11d6af9cc989ca984bc11e.png

Finally, the internal insulation and wall coverings are added, with the only trace left of the titanium framework being the metal doorframe itself. I felt it was important to leave bare as much of the framework as was practical, to help tie it into the ship's design in a very physical way, and also to remind people that there's a lot of detail hidden behind the walls that remain unseen most of the time.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40608420/c56eda9288459f9ce64a135a5b31afb9c4188a4d.png
